articles.title: Alcaraz sobrevive a un apagón y sigue luchando por París
articles.standfirst: Tuvo bolas de partido en contra pero ganó a Fritz en tres sets para pasar a semifinales
articles.summary: Tuvo bolas de partido en contra pero ganó a Fritz en tres sets para pasar a semifinales
articles.body: Parecía que Taylor Fritz iba a hacer en los cuartos de final del Masters 1.000 de París lo que tenía que hacer y Carlos Alcaraz no iba a ser capaz de hacerlo. Pero al final se llegó al resultado teóricamente lógico por un camino tortuoso que generó un partido apasionante, quizá no el mejor que pueden jugar Alcaraz y Fritz, pero sí sumamente apasionante y competido. Y al final lo ganó Alcaraz por 6-7 (10), 7-5 y 6-3 en 164 minutos de juego gracias, sobre todo, a mantenerse sereno aún cuando el juego no le acompañaba. Eso sí. Será conveniente que en su semifinal ante Casper Ruud o Nuno Borges, consiga que no se repita lo visto ante Taylor Fritz. Porque esta vez bordeó el abismo pero no cayó, pero otra vez podría no tener tanta suerte, aunque la busque como en este partido. El estadounidense es uno de los mejores sacadores del mundo mientras el español es un número 1 mundial, aunque actualmente no ocupe la plaza. En teoría el partido dependería de quién fuera capaz de llevar el partido a su terreno y el primero en hacerlo fue el estadounidense mientras Carlos también lo hizo, pero no era capaz de mantener el partido en ese punto. Fritz empezó ganando nueve puntos seguidos con su servicio -dos juegos en blanco- pero el primero que consiguió Carlos fue preludio de un 'break' que luego prolongó hasta un 5-3 y saque que parecía poner la primera manga en su mano, porque el partido estaba respondiendo a la teoría: con bola en juego y punto más largo Carlos era superior y estaba consiguiendo restar a Taylor y poner en juego la bola. Pero ahí llegó el gran apagón: perdió dos juegos consecutivos en blanco y el primero, con su servicio. Llegó un tie break en el que tuvo 4-2 de ventaja y luego varios puntos de set a favor y en contra, pero en el que cometió errores poco esperables en él. Pero antes esos apagones les costaban partidos. Ahora no tanto. Carlos nunca se desesperó, al menos visiblemente, y esperó su oportunidad con disciplina. Y Carlos Alcaraz consiguió que el partido volviera a su terreno. Se siguió jugando puntos cortos, con poco ritmo, y Taylor ejecutaba solventemente lo que mejor sabe, sacar, y además empezó a jugar de forma más versátil. Carlos cedió su servicio con 3-3 en el segundo set y tuvo luego una bola de break que no pudo aprovechar. Con 3-5, y sacando, salvó puntos de partido con el juego de fantasía que sabe desarrollar, pero sólo le valía para salvar su servicio... ...Y para seguir en el partido. Porque Carlos consiguió recuperar el break para ponerse 5-5, seguir en el partido y llevarse la segunda manga por 7-5 -es decir, ganar tres juegos consecutivos- y ya poder desarrollar un juego más parecido al habitualmente suyo. Podría decirse que cuando Taylor sacaba para ganar con 5-4 le tembló un poco la mano -igual que a Carlos en el primer set-, pero había que estar ahí para aprovecharlo. El tercer set no fue sencillo para Carlos. Se siguió jugando a tirones, sin gran ritmo y Fritz distaba de venirse abajo, pero Carlos había recuperado la seguridad y aunque Carlos rompió pronto, Taylor tuvo también opciones de recuperar el 'break'. Pero la fortaleza mental y la concentración de Carlos ya no volvieron a abandonarle. En otros encuentros de cuartos, Shelton venció a Tommy Paul 6-4, 4-6 y 6-3 y Van Assche a Hijikata 6-4, 6-7, 7-5. Luego jugarán Ruud y Nuno Borges por enfrentarse a Alcaraz.

articles.title: Rafa Jódar llega a las ATP Finals en su primer año como profesional
articles.standfirst: Se convierte en el decimosexto tenista español en jugar el torneo de los maestros
articles.summary: Se convierte en el decimosexto tenista español en jugar el torneo de los maestros
articles.body: La temporada 2026 quedará para siempre ligada a la figura de Rafa Jódar. Tras la victoria de Carlos Alcaraz ante Taylor Fritz en los cuartos de final del Masters 1000 de París, el madrileño, a sus 20 años, se convierte en el primer tenista en la historia en clasificarse a las Nitto ATP Finals en su primer año como profesional. La última edición donde hubo dos españoles en el torneo de los ocho mejores del año fue la de 2015, que juntó a Rafa Nadal y David Ferrer. A Rafa le hacía falta una carambola de casualidades para poder estar del 15 al 22 de este mes en Turín. Con las derrotas del miércoles de De Miñaur y Djokovic, el español necesitaba las eliminaciones de Tommy Paul y Taylor Fritz (el primero antes de la final y el segundo, de la semifinal). Hoy se han cumplido estas dos últimas condiciones de la mano de su compañero de equipo de Copa Davis, Carlos Alcaraz. Se une por tanto a Alexander Zverev, Carlos Alcaraz, Ben Shelton, Daniil Medvedev, Flavio Cobolli, Arthur Fils y Frances Tiafoe en el torneo de maestros. En su primera temporada como profesional firma un historial momentáneo de 45 victorias por 18 derrotas. El título conseguido el 5 de abril en Marrakech afirma su condición de campeón ATP. Además de alcanzar hasta en cuatro ocasiones los cuartos de final en torneos de categoría 1000, el último, la final de Shanghái ante Davidovich. Hace siete días se convirtió en el vigesimoprimer español en la historia en entrar al top10 del ranking ATP, tardando tan solo 287 días en hacerlo desde su debut como profesional. Otro récord de precocidad del que se adueñó Jódar, ya que superó al brasileño Gustavo Kuerten, que fijaba la marca en 490 días. Ya son 16 los tenistas españoles que se han clasificado alguna vez en su historia para la Copa de Maestros: Manuel Orantes, Emilio Sánchez Vicario, José Higueras, Sergi Bruguera, Alberto Berasategui, Albert Costa, Carlos Moyá, Alex Corretja, Tommy Robredo, Juan Carlos Ferrero, Rafa Nadal, David Ferrer, Fernando Verdasco, Pablo Carreño, Carlos Alcaraz y hoy, Rafa Jódar, ha añadido su nombre a la laureada lista. Manuel Orantes y Alex Corretja son los únicos que han podido traer el título a España.

articles.title: Paris Masters: Taylor Fritz squanders match points against Carlos Alcaraz as defeat ends hopes of reaching ATP Finals
articles.summary: Season-ending ATP Finals live on Sky Sports from November 15-22, with Spanish youngster Rafael Jodar taking eighth and final spot after Taylor Fritz's defeat to already-qualified Carlos Alcaraz in Paris; Frances Tiafoe's place secured earlier on Friday
articles.body:
Fritz would have reached the end-of-season event in Italy at Rafael Jodar's expense had he beaten Alcaraz to make the last four.

He looked poised to do that after twice finding himself a point from victory in the second set, once on his opponent's serve at 5-3 up and then on his own with the score at 5-4.

However, Alcaraz rallied during a high-quality match to triumph 6-7 (10-12) 7-5 6-3 and ensure he will be joined by compatriot Jodar at the ATP Finals from November 15-22, live on Sky Sports .

Tommy Paul's three-set defeat to fellow American Ben Shelton earlier in the day - US Open finalist Shelton prevailing 6-4 4-6 6-3 - had ended his hopes of reaching the ATP Finals, with countryman Frances Tiafoe's place subsequently secured.

Fritz was looking to become the third US representative in this year's Turin showpiece, after Shelton and Tiafoe, but squandered a golden opportunity to get there and also defeat Alcaraz for just the second time in eight attempts.

The 29-year-old won the first set after a lengthy tie-break and then broke Alcaraz to open up a 4-3 lead in the second set, before saving a break point to make that 5-3.

Alcaraz had already qualified for the ATP Finals - an event he is yet to win in three previous tries - alongside world No 1 Alexander Zverev, Daniil Medvedev, Flavio Cobolli, Arthur Fils, Shelton and Tiafoe.

Home hopes in Turin will rest on Cobolli, with Jannik Sinner - who on Friday announced a split with coach Darren Cahill after five years - ending his campaign early due to a knee problem that has sidelined him since winning Wimbledon in July.

Alcaraz will face Casper Ruud in the semi-finals in Paris after the Norwegian saw off Portugal's Nuno Borges 7-6 (7-5) 6-4, with Shelton meeting home player Luca Van Assche, who overcame Australian qualifier - and Novak Djokovic's conqueror - Rinky Hijikata 6-4 6-7 (4-7) 7-5.

Should we get an Alcaraz-Shelton final in France, it would be a repeat of their five-set epic in the US Open quarter-finals, a match Shelton won in a final-set tie-break at Flushing Meadows.

Alcaraz said after fighting back against Fritz: "I tried not to let myself down in those difficult moments - to stay strong mentally.

"We played incredible tennis, both of us, and I used the energy of the people to give them what they wanted to watch. To entertain them."

articles.title: WTA chair apologises to Jessica Pegula after airing of 'diva' comment
articles.summary: WTA chair Valerie Camillo apologises to Jessica Pegula after her "diva" comment about Mirra Andreeva was live-streamed.
articles.body:
Women's Tennis Association chair Valerie Camillo has apologised to Jessica Pegula and said the live-streaming of private comments to her coach about fellow player Mirra Andreeva was "regrettable and unacceptable".

American Pegula called Andreeva a "diva" in a private conversation with her coach after a practice session for the WTA Tour Finals on Wednesday.

However, the comments were aired on a live stream after the WTA failed to tell players there were microphones on practice courts.

World number five Pegula called the incident "unfortunate" and said the WTA players' council supported players' calls for more privacy.

Camillo said that all audio recording equipment in practice areas had since been removed as "clearly there was a failure in our technical execution and monitoring".

"I want to specifically apologise to Jessica Pegula and [coach] Mark Knowles," she added.

"What happened was regrettable and unacceptable. Jess is one of the WTA's best advocates and biggest stars. She does not deserve this distraction."

WTA takes responsibility after Pegula 'diva' comment live-streamed

Pegula was also heard saying French Open champion Andreeva "needs to be humbled" and her coach Conchita Martinez encourages her behaviour.

A representative for Pegula said she had been in direct contact with those involved and had been "completely unaware" the conversation could be heard by courtside microphones.

None of the players were asked about the incident in the pre-tournament news conference at Indian Wells on Friday, but Pegula did address it in an interview with ESPN.

"I think it's something that we have fought a lot over the last couple years as there's a lot more surveillance and audio and access to the players at tournaments than there has been in the past," she said. , external

"I know for broadcasting that it's great for fans, but I think we've seen a couple incidents now throughout the year, [the] last couple of years really, where it just seems highly unnecessary.

"I think [this will] definitely reignite the topic and, hopefully, we can unfortunately use this incident to keep pushing for more player privacy."

Pegula's compatriot Coco Gauff called for more privacy after she was captured in the players' area smashing a racquet following a defeat by Elina Svitolina in the Australian Open quarter-finals in January.

At the same major, six-time Grand Slam champion Iga Swiatek said players were being watched "like animals in the zoo" by behind-the-scenes cameras.

YouTube streams of Wednesday's practice sessions at Indian Wells have since been removed by the WTA, but the footage had already been shared on social media.

Referring to the incident in California, where the season-ending WTA Finals are being held, Camillo added: "The WTA is sensitive to player privacy and has policies and procedures in place to balance players' needs for safe spaces with opportunities to bring fans closer to the game.

"There was a lack of advanced notice and clear signage to assist players about the recording equipment operating in the area."

articles.title: WTA chair apologises to Jessica Pegula after airing of 'diva' comment about Mirra Andreeva, confirms audio deactivated on practice courts at Indian Wells
articles.summary: Jessica Pegula was heard saying Mirra Andreeva needed to be "humbled" during a practice session ahead of the WTA Finals in California; American hopes incident can help players to "keep pushing for more privacy"; watch tournament from Sunday, live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
US player Pegula describing Russian teenager Andreeva as "a diva" while conversing with coach Mark Knowles during a practice session were heard on a YouTube livestream at Indian Wells, the venue for the WTA Tour season-ending event from November 8-15.

The WTA shouldered the blame for failing to properly inform players about active microphones, with chair Valerie Camillo saying there was "a lack of advanced notice and clear signage" as she confirmed audio will now be switched off for practice sessions.

Camillo added: "I want to specifically apologise to Jessica Pegula and [coach] Mark Knowles. What happened was regrettable and unacceptable.

"Jess is one of the WTA's best advocates and biggest stars. She does not deserve this distraction.

"As a member ​organisation, one of the primary responsibilities of the WTA is to protect ​players whenever possible. The players deserve better and we will continue to work to raise the bar for the WTA."

Pegula: Let's keep pushing for more privacy

Pegula, who was also heard saying French Open champion Andreeva "needs to be humbled" and that her coach, former Wimbledon winner, Conchita Martinez, encouraged her player's behaviour, addressed the incident on ESPN on Friday.

The world No 5 said: "Obviously I had no idea and was not informed that audio was being recorded. But it is what it is.

"I think it's something that we have fought a lot over the last couple years as there's a lot more surveillance, audio and, I guess, access to the players at tournaments than there has been in the past.

"I know for broadcasting that it's great for fans, but I think we've seen a couple incidents now throughout the year, the last couple of years really, where it seems highly unnecessary.

"I think [this will] definitely reignite the topic. Hopefully we can use this incident to keep pushing for more player privacy."

Two-time Grand Slam champion Coco Gauff - in Pegula's group at the WTA Finals, alongside Linda Noskova and world No 1 Elena Rybakina - called for more privacy in January after cameras caught her smashing her racket following defeat to Elina Svitolina at the Australian Open quarter-finals in Melbourne.

articles.title: What Carlos Alcaraz said to Taylor Fritz after eliminating him from ATP Finals contention
articles.summary: Fritz came out on the short end of a highly competitive match where he had two match points
articles.body:
Taylor Fritz had two match points on Carlos Alcaraz on Friday in his Paris Masters quarterfinal. He had taken the first set in a marathon tiebreaker and had all of the momentum leading 5-3 in the second set.

Then, as if a light switch went off, Alcaraz raised his level and got the crowd involved. Fritz needed the win to qualify for the ATP Finals, but 2 hours and 45 minutes later, it was not to be, as Alcaraz won the match in three sets, 6-7, 7-5, 6-3.

The quality of the tennis was high, but many were sad for Fritz who came so close to making the ATP Finals in a year where he battled a knee injury that kept him out of the game for some time. Alcaraz was well aware of what was on the line for Fritz and was ready to talk about it when they met at the net after match point.

The first Alcaraz said to Sinner was that he was sorry. Fritz smiled at him and said he was too good.

Sportsmanship personified between two players who produced a high level of tennis in a grueling match.

This loss will sting for Fritz, but he knows how to manage the emotional highs and lows of the game.

Tommy Paul also knocked out of ATP Finals

Paul lost to Ben Shelton , who finishes the year as the top ranked American for the first time, in Paris ending his bid to make the ATP Finals.

He seemed unbothered about the outcome, either way. His offseason plan was to go fishing . After an eleven month season and a post Wimbledon wedding to longtime girlfriend Paige Lorenze , Paul is ready for some downtime.

Shelton and Frances Tiafoe are the American singles qualifiers for the ATP Finals in Turin. It is Tiafoe's first time playing in the event which features the eight highest ranked players of the 2026 season.
